sar.hook: Some places satellites almost never photograph.

scenes.caption: Rainforests sit under cloud about 300 days a year.
But radar, or SAR, makes its own light, at a wavelength clouds ignore.
So it maps the ground day, night, and straight through storms.

sar.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

mercator.hook: Every world map you have seen is lying to you.

scenes.caption: On the Mercator map, Greenland looks as big as all of Africa.
But switch to an equal-area map, and Africa is fourteen times larger.
Flattening a round planet always distorts. The only question is who gets shrunk.

mercator.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

geoai.hook: Artificial intelligence now maps every building on Earth.

scenes.caption: It reads satellite images and traces their footprints, over a billion of them.
Places once blank on the map suddenly have detail.
That is the power of geospatial machine learning, turning raw pixels into maps at planetary scale.

geoai.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

scenes.caption: Sentinel, Landsat and MODIS give decades of imagery, all free and open.
Copernicus elevation, WorldPop, WorldCover and SoilGrids are free too.
The barrier is not the data anymore. It is knowing what to ask.

datascience.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

cameroon.hook: One country is called Africa in miniature.

scenes.caption: Cameroon packs rainforest, savanna, mountains and desert into one border.
From the Atlantic coast to the edge of Lake Chad, it holds a continent in miniature.
That is why so many geographers study it first.

cameroon.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

projections.hook: There is no such thing as a perfect map.

scenes.caption: To flatten a round planet, you must cut it and stretch it somewhere.
Move the cut, and every country changes size and shape.
There is no perfect flat map. Only the right one for the job.

projections.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

nightlights.hook: You can measure an economy from space.

scenes.caption: At night, satellites see our lights, and where they grow, economies grow.
When the lights go dark, they record blackouts, conflict and collapse.
Light becomes data, even where no official statistics exist.

nightlights.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

ndvi.hook: A satellite can see a plant get sick before you can.

scenes.caption: Healthy leaves reflect invisible near-infrared light. Stressed leaves do not.
One ratio of that light, called N-D-V-I, maps plant health across whole countries.
Weeks before a drought shows on the ground, it shows from orbit.

ndvi.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

gps.hook: GPS has no idea where you are.

scenes.caption: Each satellite only broadcasts one thing, the exact time.
Your phone measures the tiny delay from several satellites at once.
Then it solves for the single point where all their signals agree.

gps.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

floodai.hook: AI can now map a flood while it is still rising.

scenes.caption: Radar satellites see through storm clouds to the water below.
Machine learning turns each pass into a live flood map.
Responders learn which roads and villages are cut off, within hours.

floodai.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

cropai.hook: An algorithm is watching every farm on Earth.

scenes.caption: Satellites revisit each field every few days.
AI flags stress, disease and drought before the harvest fails.
For smallholder farmers, that early warning can save the season.

cropai.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

crsbug.hook: One setting has ruined more maps than any other bug.

scenes.caption: It is the coordinate reference system, the C-R-S.
Mix two of them, and your data quietly lands in the wrong place.
The code runs fine. The map is just wrong. Always check your CRS.

crsbug.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

redriver.hook: This river floods every spring because it flows the wrong way.

scenes.caption: Most rivers flow toward the equator. The Red River flows north.
In spring the warm southern end thaws while the north is still frozen.
The meltwater has nowhere to go, so the flat valley floods.

redriver.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

drought.hook: We can see a drought coming before a single leaf turns brown.

scenes.caption: Long before plants brown, they lose moisture you cannot see.
A satellite index called N-D-M-I tracks that water, weeks ahead.
That head start is time to warn farmers and move water.

drought.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

clinic.hook: The clinic is five kilometres away. It might as well be a hundred.

scenes.caption: Straight-line distance ignores the one thing that matters, the road.
Map the real road network, and five kilometres can mean a three-hour journey.
That gap decides who reaches care in time.

clinic.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

urbanheat.hook: Your city is hotter than the countryside, and it is by design.

scenes.caption: Asphalt and dark roofs soak up heat all day long.
At night they release it, keeping cities up to seven degrees warmer.
Thirty years of satellite data show it getting worse, block by block.

urbanheat.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

antipodes.hook: Dig straight down through the Earth and you would not reach China.

scenes.caption: The point exactly opposite yours is called your antipode.
For most of the United States, that point is in the Indian Ocean.
Two-thirds of all land has ocean on the other side. Earth is mostly water.

antipodes.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

northup.hook: There is no real reason north has to be up.

scenes.caption: Space has no up. Old maps put east, or even south, at the top.
North-up became standard only with the compass and European mapmaking.
Flip the map and the same world suddenly feels unfamiliar. That is a choice, not a law.

northup.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

utm.hook: Every GPS point you have ever used sits on a hidden grid.

scenes.caption: Latitude and longitude are angles, not meters. Hard to measure distance with.
So we slice the planet into 60 flat zones, each with its own metre grid: U-T-M.
It is why your survey lines up on the ground, and why the zone must match.

utm.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

deforestation.hook: You can watch a forest disappear from space, almost in real time.

scenes.caption: Satellites revisit the Amazon every few days and flag pixels that turned from green to bare.
The signature is unmistakable: sharp straight edges and a fishbone of new roads.
Alerts now reach rangers within days, turning maps into enforcement.

deforestation.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

aurora.hook: Satellites see the northern lights from above.

scenes.caption: The aurora is the solar wind slamming into our magnetic field, 100 kilometres up.
From orbit, it is a glowing green ribbon wrapped around the pole.
The same space weather that paints it can knock out GPS and power grids.

aurora.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

wildfire.hook: A satellite can spot a wildfire before anyone calls it in.

scenes.caption: Thermal sensors detect the heat signature of a fire just a few metres across.
They map the smoke plume and the active fire front several times a day.
That head start is what buys evacuation time.

wildfire.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

sam.hook: One AI model can now outline every object in a satellite image.

scenes.caption: Foundation models learned the shape of things: fields, buildings, ponds, roads.
Point at a lake and it traces the whole shoreline in one click.
Mapping that took analysts weeks now takes minutes.

sam.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

roadai.hook: AI is tracing every road on Earth from orbit.

scenes.caption: Many maps still have blank spots where no one has surveyed the roads.
Models trained on satellite imagery draw the missing network automatically.
For disaster response, a current road map is the difference between reaching people or not.

roadai.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

cog.hook: You can read one corner of a 100-gigabyte satellite image without downloading it.

scenes.caption: A cloud-optimized GeoTIFF stores the file so any tile can be fetched on its own.
Your code asks for just the pixels in view, over the network, in milliseconds.
Petabytes of imagery become something a laptop can actually work with.

cog.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

spatialjoin.hook: One line of geospatial code can freeze your laptop for an hour.

scenes.caption: A spatial join checks every shape against every other shape. That is millions times millions.
A spatial index sorts the data by location first, so each shape only checks its neighbours.
Same answer, a thousand times faster. Indexing is the whole game.

spatialjoin.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

himalaya.hook: The tallest mountains on Earth are still growing, and satellites can measure it.

scenes.caption: India is still crashing into Asia, lifting the Himalaya a few millimetres a year.
Radar satellites measure that ground motion from orbit, to the millimetre.
The same technique tracks sinking cities and slipping faults before a quake.

himalaya.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

bluemarble.hook: The most reproduced photograph in history is a map.

scenes.caption: In 1972 the Apollo 17 crew shot the whole Earth, lit and round, in one frame.
For the first time people saw the planet with no borders drawn on it.
Every basemap you scroll today is the descendant of that single view.

bluemarble.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

greatcircle.hook: The shortest flight path looks like a curve on your map.

scenes.caption: On a globe, the straight line between two cities bends toward the pole.
Flatten that globe onto a map and the same straight path looks curved.
It is why flights from the US to Asia arc up over the Arctic.

greatcircle.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

dateline.hook: Cross one invisible line in the Pacific and it is suddenly tomorrow.

scenes.caption: The International Date Line runs down the middle of the Pacific.
Step across it going west and you skip a whole day forward.
It zig-zags around islands so each nation keeps a single date.

dateline.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

equator.hook: Standing on the equator, you are spinning at 1,600 kilometres an hour.

scenes.caption: Earth turns once a day, and the equator is the widest circle around it.
So the ground there races eastward far faster than at the poles.
That free eastward speed is exactly why rockets launch near the equator.

equator.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

straightborders.hook: Some country borders are just straight lines a ruler drew.

scenes.caption: Rivers and mountains make crooked borders. Straight ones are drawn by people.
Much of Africa's map was ruled off in European capitals in the 1880s.
Those lines still cut through peoples and rivers today.

straightborders.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

tiles.hook: Every online map is really millions of tiny square images.

scenes.caption: Zoom in and the map quietly swaps in sharper 256-pixel tiles.
Each zoom level has four times as many tiles as the one before.
That pyramid of tiles is why a world map loads instantly on your phone.

tiles.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

geocoding.hook: Turning an address into a dot on the map is harder than it sounds.

scenes.caption: People write addresses a hundred messy ways. Computers need one exact point.
Geocoding matches the text to a known location, then guesses the rest.
Get it wrong and your delivery, or your ambulance, goes to the wrong street.

geocoding.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

bigdata.hook: One day of satellite imagery is bigger than the entire early internet.

scenes.caption: Earth-observing satellites now stream terabytes of pixels every single day.
No one downloads it all. You send the code to the data, in the cloud.
Platforms like Earth Engine turn a planet of pixels into one line of code.

bigdata.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

hurricane.hook: A satellite watches the eye of a hurricane form in real time.

scenes.caption: From orbit, the storm is a perfect spiral with a calm eye at its centre.
Satellites clock its winds, path and pressure hours before landfall.
That warning is measured in lives, not likes.

hurricane.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

glacier.hook: Satellites watch a glacier retreat, one summer at a time.

scenes.caption: Line up images across the years and the ice visibly pulls back.
Meltwater carves bright blue lakes and rivers across the white.
The record is undeniable because it is the same camera, year after year.

glacier.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

dust.hook: Desert dust crosses an entire ocean to feed a rainforest.

scenes.caption: Every year the Sahara lofts millions of tonnes of dust into the sky.
Satellites track the plume as it drifts across the Atlantic.
It lands on the Amazon, carrying the very phosphorus the forest needs.

dust.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

sealevel.hook: Satellites measure the height of the ocean to the width of a finger.

scenes.caption: A radar altimeter bounces a pulse off the sea and times the echo.
Repeat it for 30 years and you can see the ocean slowly rising.
For low coasts and deltas, a few centimetres decides who floods.

sealevel.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

changedetection.hook: AI can tell you exactly what changed between two satellite passes.

scenes.caption: Take the same place on two dates and subtract one image from the other.
A model flags only the meaningful change: new clearing, new water, new building.
It turns a firehose of imagery into a short list of what actually matters.

changedetection.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

lesotho.hook: One country is completely enclosed by another, and it is not a tiny city-state.

scenes.caption: Vatican City and San Marino are famous enclaves, but Lesotho is a full nation of two million people.
Lesotho sits entirely inside South Africa, a mountain kingdom with no coastline of its own.
Drive in any direction to leave the country, and you cross straight into South Africa.

lesotho.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

landsat.hook: One satellite program has been photographing the same ground every couple of weeks for over fifty years.

scenes.caption: Landsat 1 launched in 1972 and began the longest continuous space record of Earth's land surface.
Today Landsat 8 and 9 fly together, revisiting any point on Earth every eight days.
That unbroken archive lets scientists watch forests, cities and coastlines change decade by decade.

landsat.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

deepfakegeo.hook: In 2021, researchers proved AI could fake a satellite photo of a place, complete with buildings and rivers that were never there.

scenes.caption: The study used a generative AI model to swap real features between different cities' satellite scenes.
The output looked like ordinary satellite imagery, but showed structures and terrain that did not exist on the ground.
Geographers now call this risk deep fake geography, a warning to verify imagery before trusting it.

deepfakegeo.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

popai.hook: AI can estimate how many people live in a village that has never been surveyed.

scenes.caption: Machine-learning models scan satellite images to spot individual buildings, roof by roof.
Combined with known census patterns, that building count becomes a population estimate for places no census reached.
Aid agencies use these AI-built population maps to plan vaccine drives and disaster relief.

popai.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

nullisland.hook: Thousands of GPS errors all point to the exact same empty spot in the ocean.

scenes.caption: It is where the equator crosses the prime meridian, coordinates zero, zero exactly.
When location software fails, it often defaults to that same zero-zero point instead of nothing.
Mapmakers nicknamed it Null Island, and a real ocean buoy floats there today.

nullisland.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

hexgrid.hook: Some data scientists redraw the entire planet in hexagons before they run a single query.

scenes.caption: In a square grid, four neighbours touch an edge and four touch only a corner, so nearby is not one distance.
A hexagon's six neighbours are all the same distance away, so nearby means the same thing everywhere on the grid.
Uber open-sourced this hex grid, called H3, and it now bins millions of GPS pings in seconds.

hexgrid.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

doublelandlocked.hook: Only two countries on Earth are landlocked by other landlocked countries.

scenes.caption: Liechtenstein sits wedged between Switzerland and Austria, and both of those are landlocked too.
Uzbekistan is ringed by five neighbours, and every single one is also landlocked.
From either country, reaching open ocean means crossing at least two borders no matter which way you go.

doublelandlocked.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

triplefrontier.hook: Stand on one riverbank and you can look into three different countries at once.

scenes.caption: The Iguazu River flows into the Parana River, and that confluence is where three borders meet.
Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay all touch this one triangle of water, no bridge or fence needed to see all three.
Locals call it the Triple Frontier, one of the few places on Earth where three nations share a single point.

triplefrontier.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

methaneleak.hook: A satellite can catch a gas leak that the company never reported.

hookImg.commons: oil and gas field aerial photo

scenes.caption: Methane is invisible to our eyes, but it absorbs one very specific band of infrared light.
Instruments like Europe's Sentinel-5P scan the whole planet every day, watching for that exact signature.
In 2022 that scanning exposed undisclosed 'super-emitter' leaks at oil and gas sites in Central Asia.

methaneleak.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

povertyai.hook: An AI once estimated how poor a village was from nothing but a satellite photo.

scenes.caption: Household surveys are slow and costly, so most villages on Earth have never been formally surveyed.
Researchers trained a model to link daytime imagery to nighttime light levels, a known proxy for economic activity.
Its estimates lined up closely with real household survey data, offering a way to map poverty where no survey exists.

povertyai.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

buildingheight.hook: AI can now guess how tall a building is from a completely flat satellite photo.

scenes.caption: A standard satellite photo has no height data, just a flat grid of coloured pixels.
Models learn to read shadow length and rooftop shape as clues to how tall each structure really is.
Google's Open Buildings project used this method to map building heights across Africa where no ground survey ever existed.

buildingheight.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

srtm.hook: One 11-day space shuttle mission mapped the elevation of most of Earth's land.

scenes.caption: In February 2000, Space Shuttle Endeavour flew two radar antennas, one in the cargo bay and one on a 60-metre mast.
The tiny difference between what each antenna received let software calculate the elevation of the ground below.
In just 11 days, the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission mapped elevation for about 80 percent of Earth's land surface.

srtm.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

kaliningrad.hook: One piece of Russia has no land border with the rest of Russia.

scenes.caption: After 1945 the German city of Konigsberg became Soviet Kaliningrad, cut off from the Russian mainland by newly independent states.
Today it sits on the Baltic Sea wedged between Poland and Lithuania, over 300 kilometres from mainland Russia by land.
To drive there from Moscow, you have to cross the territory of at least one other country first.

kaliningrad.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

icesat.hook: A NASA satellite measures the height of Earth's ice by counting single photons.

scenes.caption: ICESat-2's laser fires ten thousand pulses a second and times individual photons bouncing back from the surface.
That timing lets it measure surface height to within a few centimetres, on repeat passes over the same ground.
Stacked year after year, those measurements reveal exactly how fast Greenland and Antarctica's ice is thinning.

icesat.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

coralbleach.hook: Satellites can warn that a reef is about to bleach before a single diver sees it turn white.

scenes.caption: Warm water stresses coral into expelling the colourful algae that feed it, leaving the skeleton bare and white.
NOAA satellites track sea-surface temperature worldwide and flag reefs under heat stress in near real time.
That satellite-built bleaching alert gives reef managers weeks of warning before the damage is visible underwater.

coralbleach.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

darkships.hook: AI can spot a ship that is trying to hide from satellites.

scenes.caption: Most ships broadcast their position automatically, but some switch that signal off to fish illegally or dodge sanctions.
Radar satellites see every vessel anyway, transponder or not, because a metal hull bounces a strong signal straight back.
AI models scan those radar images and match each unlisted ship's track, mapping vessels that never meant to be seen.

darkships.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

wildlifeai.hook: Researchers once counted a herd of elephants from space, without a single ranger on the ground.

scenes.caption: High-resolution satellites can resolve an object the size of an elephant clearly enough to make out its shape and shadow.
Researchers trained a deep learning model on thousands of labelled images to pick those shapes out automatically.
The model matched trained human counters, letting scientists survey herds across huge, hard-to-reach landscapes from orbit.

wildlifeai.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

voronoi.hook: One geometric trick decides which hospital is really your nearest one.

scenes.caption: Give a map a set of points, like hospitals, and a Voronoi diagram draws the boundary where you are closer to one than any other.
Each resulting cell is a catchment area: every location inside it is nearest to that one point, not the others.
GIS analysts use these cells to plan service areas, from clinics and fire stations to cell towers and delivery zones.

voronoi.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

pointnemo.hook: When the space station flies overhead, it is closer to one point in the ocean than any person standing on land.

scenes.caption: Point Nemo sits in the South Pacific, more than 2,600 kilometers from the nearest shore in every direction.
The International Space Station orbits about 400 kilometers up, closer to that spot than the nearest coastline.
Space agencies also aim retired satellites and cargo spacecraft at this same empty water on purpose.

pointnemo.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

gracewater.hook: Twin satellites can tell a region lost its groundwater just by weighing it from orbit.

scenes.caption: Two satellites named GRACE flew in tight formation, sensing tiny shifts in Earth's own gravity.
When underground water drains away, the ground loses mass, and the satellites feel the pull change.
That let scientists measure aquifers draining faster than rainfall could refill them, without drilling a single well.

gracewater.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

swot.hook: One satellite launched in 2022 is the first to measure the height of nearly every river and lake on Earth.

scenes.caption: Most rivers on Earth had never been measured for water surface height in one consistent global survey.
SWOT bounces radar across a wide swath, mapping the elevation of water surfaces down to a few centimeters.
That single instrument now tracks flood risk and drought stress on rivers and lakes worldwide.

swot.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

solarai.hook: One AI model mapped every solar panel in the United States from aerial photos alone.

scenes.caption: Spotting every rooftop solar panel from satellite images by eye would take an army of analysts.
Researchers trained a deep learning model to recognize the shape and glare of solar panels instead.
It mapped 1.47 million installations across the country, the first fine grained national solar census.

solarai.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

climatetrace.hook: A coalition of AI models now tracks greenhouse gas emissions from individual power plants and factories worldwide.

scenes.caption: Governments and companies self-report most emissions data, and those numbers are often years old or missing.
Climate TRACE instead reads satellite imagery of smoke, flares and heat, then lets AI estimate the emissions directly.
It was unveiled at a United Nations climate summit, offering an independent check on what polluters actually report.

climatetrace.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

geohash.hook: A short string like 9q8yyk can pinpoint a location on Earth, and its own length decides how precise it is.

scenes.caption: Latitude and longitude are two long decimal numbers, awkward to store, sort or search together.
A geohash interleaves their digits into one short string, so nearby places share the same starting letters.
Trim the last character and the same string still points to the same neighborhood, just less precisely.

geohash.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

birtawil.hook: One patch of desert on Earth belongs to no country at all.

scenes.caption: Egypt and Sudan drew two different border lines in 1899 and 1902, and the two versions disagree over two patches of land.
Both countries claim the coastal Halaib Triangle nearby, but each claim requires giving up Bir Tawil, the desert patch next to it.
So neither country will claim Bir Tawil, leaving about 2,060 square kilometers unclaimed by any nation on Earth.

birtawil.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

baarle.hook: One European town has a national border running straight through people's living rooms.

scenes.caption: Baarle-Hertog is Belgian territory scattered across more than twenty separate patches inside the Netherlands.
Some of those Belgian patches even contain smaller Dutch patches inside them, enclaves within enclaves.
White crosses set into the pavement trace the line, and in places it runs straight through houses and shops.

baarle.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

volcanoinsar.hook: Satellites can watch a volcano start to swell months before it erupts.

scenes.caption: As magma rises underground, it pushes the surface above it upward by centimeters, too subtle to see by eye.
Radar satellites compare images of the same volcano from different days and measure that tiny swelling.
That technique, called InSAR, now gives scientists warning of many eruptions before the first plume ever appears.

volcanoinsar.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

dscovr.hook: One NASA camera keeps a live photo of the whole sunlit Earth, taken from a million miles away.

scenes.caption: DSCOVR sits at a gravitational balance point between Earth and the Sun called Lagrange point one, about a million miles out.
From there its EPIC camera always faces the fully lit side of Earth, a view no satellite closer to us can hold.
It captures a new full Earth image roughly every one to two hours and posts it publicly the same day.

dscovr.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

photogeo.hook: An AI can now guess where an ordinary photo was taken with no location data attached at all.

scenes.caption: Researchers trained a model on millions of geotagged street level photos, without ever telling it a single rule of geography.
It learned instead from clues like road markings, plants, architecture and even the angle of the shadows.
In head to head tests, it placed random photos closer to the true location than most human players of location guessing games.

photogeo.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.

raycast.hook: One simple trick is how your phone knows a point is inside a country and not just near it.

scenes.caption: Draw an imaginary ray from the point straight out to the edge of the map and count how many times it crosses the border.
Cross the line an odd number of times and the point is inside. Cross it an even number of times and it is outside.
That single rule, called ray casting, is what lets software test millions of points against a shape in an instant.

raycast.outro: Follow for the science behind the map.
